# Introduction to geriatrics

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Family medicine > Geriatric care > Introduction to geriatrics*

[Original Article Link](/library/On0Itg)

---

## Summary

Geriatrics is the branch of medicine concerned with the health and care of older adults, defined by the American Geriatrics Society (<u>AGS</u>) as those aged 65 years or older. Normal <u>aging changes</u> (e.g., stiffening of <u>arteries</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>, decline in cognitive function) predispose older adults to multiple chronic conditions, disability, adverse pharmacological reactions, and decreased quality of life. A comprehensive <u>geriatric assessment</u>, usually performed by a primary care physician, can help identify older adults' health care needs and develop management plans that improve their well-being. This assessment involves evaluating functional status, <u>screening for geriatric syndromes</u> (e.g., <u>frailty</u>, cognitive impairment, and <u>malnutrition</u>), providing appropriate preventive care, assessing medications, and establishing treatment goals and <u>advance directives</u>. <u>Polypharmacy</u> is common in older adults, and evaluating its effects becomes more important as they age. <u>Conservative prescribing practices</u> (assessing appropriateness before starting new medications, performing regular medication reviews, and stopping medications that are no longer indicated) can help reduce pill burden and consequences of <u>polypharmacy</u> (e.g., <u>adverse events</u> due to <u>drug interactions</u>). Older adults with significant impairment or complex care needs may require referral to a geriatrician. Depending on their current functional status and care needs, the appropriate care setting for an older adult may be a private home, a short-term post-acute care facility (an <u>acute inpatient rehabilitation facility</u> or a <u>skilled nursing facility</u>), or a long-term care facility (an <u>assisted living facility</u>, <u>nursing home</u>, or <u>long-term acute care hospital</u>).

---

## Geriatric assessment

### General principles [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)




* Usually a multidisciplinary assessment led by a primary care physician or geriatrician

* Includes typical elements of a <u>clinical examination</u> with additional emphasis on assessing functional and cognitive abilities

* Explores social and environmental factors impacting a patient's functional status





> [!TIP]
> The <u>geriatric assessment</u> can be performed over multiple scheduled visits as necessary. [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)




### Indications




* At the start of any hospital admission for older adults [[3]](/library/8o1Od30)

* Consider outpatient <u>geriatric assessment</u> if patients present with any of the following: [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)

* <u>Multimorbidity</u>

* Functional impairment

* <u>Geriatric syndromes</u>

* <u>Polypharmacy</u>

* Transitions in care settings (e.g., entering a <u>nursing home</u>)

* Concerns about social support and/or safety





> [!TIP]
> Geriatric assessments allow for the early identification and management of conditions that can impact functional status and quality of life. Therefore, they are usually inappropriate for patients with end-stage disease (e.g., advanced <u>dementia</u>, terminal cancer) or complete functional dependence. [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)




### Components




* Perform a <u>functional status assessment</u>.

* <u>Screen for geriatric syndromes</u>.

* Assess social factors.

* Provide appropriate preventive care.

* Establish a <u>care plan</u> according to the patient's needs and preferences.

* Discuss the importance of establishing timely <u>advance directives</u> regarding:

* Preferences for future medical care and interventions

* A <u>surrogate decision-maker</u>





### Referrals




* Multiple referrals, e.g., to a nutritionist, physical therapist, and social worker, are often required.

* Consider referral to a geriatrician if the patient is: [[4]](/library/uo1pd30)[[5]](/library/Eo18d30)

* Aged ≥ 85 years

* Aged < 85 years but has:

* Significant functional impairment

* A <u>geriatric syndrome</u>

* Particularly complex medical needs (e.g., involving multiple specialists, <u>polypharmacy</u>)

## Screening for geriatric syndromes

### Overview [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)[[14]](/library/itcJWV0)[[15]](/library/nU17dT0)



* Geriatric syndromes 

* A group of complex health conditions that may result from multiple <u>risk factors</u> and organ system impairments

* Makes individuals vulnerable to additional physical stressors or insults

* <u>Risk factors</u> increase with age and may include:

* Functional impairment (i.e., in <u>ADLs</u> and/or <u>IADLs</u>)

* Impaired mobility

* Cognitive impairment

> [!WARNING]
> Up to 80% of cognitive impairment diagnoses are missed by primary care physicians. [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Urinary incontinence in older adults</u> is associated with an increased risk of <u>decubitus ulcers</u>, <u>sepsis</u>, <u>renal failure</u>, <u>UTIs</u>, and <u>death</u>. [[6]](/library/8rcOQd0)




### Frailty assessment [[16]](/library/W01PU20)




Frailty is a <u>geriatric syndrome</u> that encompasses variable impairments in multiple domains (e.g., mobility, strength, <u>cognition</u>), increasing the risk of <u>morbidity</u> and mortality.  [[16]](/library/W01PU20)[[17]](/library/BAczNU0)[[18]](/library/AU1RfT0)




* Indications

* Consider for all older adults.

* Outpatient screening is particularly important for patients at increased risk, e.g.: [[16]](/library/W01PU20)

* Current or <u>former smokers</u>

* Individuals negatively impacted by <u>social determinants of health</u>

* Patients with specific comorbidities

* Screen older adults on admission to hospital to help establish prognosis and care goals. [[17]](/library/BAczNU0)

* Example screening tools

* <u>CSHA clinical frailty scale</u> [[17]](/library/BAczNU0)

* <u>FRAIL questionnaire</u> [[15]](/library/nU17dT0)[[27]](/library/fh1kWg0)

* Edmonton frail scale  [[28]](/library/Co1qV30)[[29]](/library/xo1EV30)

* Management of <u>frailty</u> [[16]](/library/W01PU20)

* Refer for a multicomponent physical activity program that includes resistance and balance training.

* Address contributors, e.g., <u>polypharmacy</u>, weight loss, fatigue.

* Consider the need for social support.





> [!TIP]
> Multiple geriatric syndromes → ↑ risk of <u>frailty</u> → ↑ risk of further geriatric syndromes → ↑ risk of disability, institutionalization, and <u>death</u>. [[14]](/library/itcJWV0)




### Falls in older adults [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)[[19]](/library/CAcqNU0)[[30]](/library/TDc6de0)




The following guidance is based on the current CDC STEADI algorithm for falls.  [[19]](/library/CAcqNU0)[[20]](/library/DS11bg0)[[31]](/library/Q2duh60)




#### Screening




* Ask all older adults annually: Have you fallen in the past year? 

* If yes: What were the circumstances of the fall(s)?

* If no, ask:

* Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking?

* Are you worried about falling?

* If yes to any question: at risk for falls; perform a <u>fall risk assessment</u>.

* If no to all questions: Recommend general fall prevention strategies (see “<u>Fall prevention in older adults</u>”).





> [!TIP]
> Older adults should be screened for fall risk annually, beginning with the question, “Have you fallen in the past year?” [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)




#### Fall risk assessment




This should be performed for patients who screen positive for fall risk or who present after an acute fall.




* Identify <u>risk factors</u>, including:

* Underlying medical conditions (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>)

* Medications associated with increased fall risk, e.g., <u>benzodiazepines</u>, <u>antidepressants</u> (see “<u>Beers Criteria</u>”)

* Environmental hazards at home (e.g., floor surface, inadequate lighting, furniture location)

* Perform a <u>physical examination</u>, including:

* Postural <u>vital signs</u> (to identify <u>orthostatic hypotension</u>)

* Musculoskeletal tests to evaluate gait, strength, and balance, e.g.: [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)

* Get up and go test

* Ask the patient to get up from a straight-backed chair, walk 3 m (10 ft), turn around, walk back, and sit down again.

* The result is abnormal if patients have qualitative impairments  or the test takes > 12 seconds.  [[32]](/library/vS1AYg0)

* <u>Performance-oriented mobility assessment</u> (<u>Tinetti test</u>) [[33]](/library/8tcO2V0)

* <u>Visual acuity testing</u>

* Feet and footwear assessment  [[20]](/library/DS11bg0)

* Consider:

* A <u>cognitive assessment</u> [[30]](/library/TDc6de0)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>, e.g.:

* <u>CBC</u> (to rule out <u>anemia</u>)

* <u>BMP</u> (to rule out <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities)

* Serum <u>vitamin B<sub>12</sub></u> level

* Serum <u>vitamin D</u> level





#### Fall prevention in older adults [[31]](/library/Q2duh60)




The aim of preventive measures is to maximize the patient's independence and safety in line with their values and preferences.




* All patients

* Provide general education, e.g., on medication interaction risks, appropriate footwear, home hazards.

* Recommend regular exercise (including aerobic, balance, and <u>strength training</u>).  [[30]](/library/TDc6de0)

* Ask about <u>vitamin D</u> intake (from diet, supplements, sunlight) and <u>risk factors for vitamin D deficiency</u>; consider recommending a supplement.  [[30]](/library/TDc6de0)[[31]](/library/Q2duh60)[[34]](/library/dS1oAT0)[[35]](/library/Fwcgke0)

* As indicated according to risk assessment

* Optimize the management of comorbidities, including medication adjustments.

* Minimize the number of medications that may contribute to falls;  (see “<u>Beers Criteria</u>” below for details).

* Refer to <u>occupational therapy</u> for a <u>home hazard assessment and modification</u>.

* Evidence of poor gait, strength, or balance: Refer for <u>physical therapy</u>.

* Consult additional specialists as required (e.g., ophthalmologist, podiatrist).

* For hospitalized patients, consider additional measures.  [[36]](/library/CgWqxk0)





> [!WARNING]
> Falls are the leading cause of injury-related <u>death</u> in adults aged ≥ 65 years. [[37]](/library/_Mb5r8)




### Neuropsychological assessment in older adults [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)




#### <u>Cognitive assessment</u>




* Indications

* Suspected <u>mild cognitive impairment</u> (<u>MCI</u>) or <u>dementia</u>

* As part of a <u>Medicare</u> <u>Annual Wellness Visit</u> [[21]](/library/LDcwUe0)[[38]](/library/2YWToP0)

* Example <u>screening tests</u>: see also “<u>Cognitive testing</u>.”

* Patient: <u>Mini-Cog</u>, <u>MoCA</u>, or <u>MMSE</u>  [[15]](/library/nU17dT0)[[21]](/library/LDcwUe0)[[39]](/library/321ShT0)

* Carer: Informant questionnaire on cognitive decline in the elderly   [[40]](/library/ko1mX30)

* Management considerations: see also “<u>Management of major neurocognitive disorder</u>.”

* Consider a diagnosis of <u>delirium</u> (instead of or in addition to <u>dementia</u>), especially in patients with acute or fluctuating symptoms.

* Early diagnosis of <u>MCI</u> is important, as interventions such as aerobic exercise may help prevent progression to <u>dementia</u> (see “<u>Prevention of dementia</u>”). [[41]](/library/3rcSSd0)

* For patients who drive and have a diagnosis of <u>MCI</u> or <u>dementia</u>, check state laws to determine if: [[15]](/library/nU17dT0)

* Patients are required to take an annual test to maintain their driver's license.

* Physicians are mandated to report <u>MCI</u> diagnoses to the Department of Motor Vehicles.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Dementia</u> affects 30% of adults aged > 85 years, but it is not part of the normal <u>aging</u> process (the term “senile <u>dementia</u>” is a misnomer) and always requires management. [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)[[42]](/library/pBcLbU0)




> [!TIP]
> Continuity of care is important for the early detection of signs of cognitive decline. [[43]](/library/kp1mp30)




![Informant Questionnaire on Cognitive Decline in the Elderly (IQCODE)](media/kspo80eyscwu3fu48lgqccf2.jpg)

Informant Questionnaire on Cognitive Decline in the Elderly (IQCODE)




#### Mood assessment




* Overview

* Clinically significant depressive symptoms affect 10–15% of older adults. [[44]](/library/yycd3U0)

* <u>Depression</u> can present in atypical ways in older adults (e.g., <u>pseudodementia</u>, <u>apathy</u>, weight loss). [[2]](/library/gIcFXd0)

* Ask the patient about <u>sleep</u> quality.  [[45]](/library/SK1yf30)

* Indication: Screen all patients annually.

* Example <u>screening tests</u>

* <u>PHQ-2</u>  (followed by <u>PHQ-9</u> if score is ≥ 3) or <u>PHQ-9</u>

* <u>GDS-15</u>   [[46]](/library/6U1jVT0)

* Management considerations: See “<u>Depression in older adults</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Cognitive impairment, decreased functional status, and <u>suicide</u> are more common in <u>older adults with depression</u> than in younger adults with <u>depression</u>. [[47]](/library/Rh1ldg0)

### Nutritional assessment




* See “<u>Nutritional assessment in older adults</u>” for screening.

* See “<u>Unintentional weight loss and malnutrition</u>” for details on diagnosis and management.





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with advanced <u>dementia</u> should be offered oral feeding with careful assistance, not placement of a percutaneous <u>feeding tube</u>. [[48]](/library/CS1qbg0)

## Principles of pharmacotherapy for older adults

* The impact of <u>aging</u> on <u>pharmacokinetics</u>  increases the likelihood of adverse drug effects and <u>drug interactions</u> in older adults (see “<u>Fundamentals of pharmacology</u>”). [[56]](/library/no17c30)

* <u>Polypharmacy</u> in older adults is common (especially in those living in long-term care facilities) because of multiple comorbidities. [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* Older age, <u>polypharmacy</u>, and <u>limited health literacy</u> all contribute to an increased risk of <u>medication errors</u>. [[58]](/library/alcQvc0)

* Follow principles of prescribing for older adults.

* Consider whether new medications are appropriate (see “Initiation of new medications”).

* Use low starting doses and titrate slowly while assessing for adverse effects. [[59]](/library/Mo1Mc30)

* Perform regular medication reviews to determine if any need to be adjusted or stopped.

* See also “<u>Prevention of medication errors</u>.”

## Beers Criteria

### Overview [[60]](/library/BPdzSJ0)




* The <u>AGS</u> <u>Beers Criteria</u> are recommendations for pharmacological care in older adults to:

* Improve medication selection

* Reduce <u>adverse events</u>

* <u>Beers Criteria</u> apply to older adults in all care settings except at the end of life (e.g., <u>hospice</u>).

* Recommendations are divided into the following categories:

* Medications to avoid in most older adults

* Medications to avoid in older adults with specific conditions (e.g., <u>heart failure</u>, history of falls)

* Medications to avoid in older adults with impaired <u>kidney function</u>

* Medications to be used with caution in older adults

* <u>Drug interactions</u>





> [!TIP]
> Many commonly prescribed drugs (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>proton pump inhibitors</u>) may be harmful in older adults.




### Selected medication recommendations [[60]](/library/BPdzSJ0)

| <u>Antihypertensives</u> | <br>* Nonselective peripheral <u>α-blockers</u>: <u>doxazosin</u>, <u>prazosin</u>, <u>terazosin</u><br><br> | <br>* Increased risk of <u>orthostatic hypotension</u><br><br> | <br>* Avoid in most older adults.<br><br> |
| <br>* Immediate-release <u>nifedipine</u><br><br> | <br>* Increased risk of <u>hypotension</u>, <u>myocardial</u> <u>ischemia</u><br><br> |  |  |

| <br>* <u>Estrogen</u> (with or without <u>progestin</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Increased risk of <u>breast</u> and <u>endometrial cancer</u><br><br> | <br>* Avoid intitiation of systemic <u>estrogen</u>; consider discontinuation if already in use.<br><br> |  |





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid use of ≥ 2 <u>anticholinergic drugs</u> in combination in most older adults, and avoid any <u>anticholinergic drugs</u> in older adults with <u>delirium</u>, <u>dementia</u>, cognitive impairment, or a history of falls or <u>fractures</u>. [[60]](/library/BPdzSJ0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid use of <u>benzodiazepines</u> and <u>nonbenzodiazepine hypnotics</u> in most older adults, including those with <u>delirium</u>, <u>dementia</u>, cognitive impairment, or a history of falls or <u>fractures</u>. [[60]](/library/BPdzSJ0)

## Management of existing medications

### Approach [[59]](/library/Mo1Mc30)[[61]](/library/5o1ic30)




* Ensure patients receive recommended monitoring.  [[61]](/library/5o1ic30)

* Perform regular medication reviews.

* Be aware of the risks of <u>polypharmacy</u>, and consider <u>deprescribing</u> when possible.





### Medication reviews




* Ask the patient to bring in all the medications they take, including over-the-counter, complementary, and alternative medications (a <u>brown bag medication review</u>).

* Review the indications for each prescribed medication, and ensure proper documentation.

* Determine if all medications are still being taken and, if so, at what dosage.

* Assess if prescribed medications:

* Are still appropriate for the patient's:

* Age (e.g., using the <u>Beers Criteria</u>).

* Condition  [[61]](/library/5o1ic30)

* Require dosage adjustments (e.g., renal dosing)

* Could cause or are causing <u>drug interactions</u>

* Have benefits that outweigh the potential harms of continued use

* Could be replaced with a more affordable formulation





> [!TIP]
> A comprehensive <u>medication review</u> should be conducted at each health maintenance visit and considered for each patient visit. [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)




### <u>Polypharmacy</u>




* Polypharmacy is the routine and concurrent use of multiple medications (usually defined as ≥ 5 medications).  [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)[[65]](/library/Oi1I7g0)

* <u>Polypharmacy</u> is associated with increased health care spending and poor patient outcomes including: [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* Falls, <u>frailty</u>, disability, and <u>death</u>

* <u>Adverse drug events</u> (e.g., due to <u>drug interactions</u> or <u>medication errors</u>)

* <u>Drug-induced cognitive impairment</u> causing toxic <u>encephalopathy</u>

* Taking medications incorrectly (e.g., missing doses, taking additional doses)





#### Factors that contribute to polypharmacy




* Patient factors [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* Age > 62 years

* Cognitive impairment, mental health conditions, or developmental disability

* Complex care needs

* No primary care physician

* Living in a long-term care facility

* Systemic factors [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* Substandard medical documentation and/or transition of care

* Use of automatic medication refills

* Prioritization of <u>quality metrics</u> that are condition-specific





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Polypharmacy</u> in older adults is associated with an increased risk of <u>adverse drug events</u>, <u>delirium</u>, falls, and cognitive and functional decline. [[48]](/library/CS1qbg0)




### How to safely deprescribe [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)[[66]](/library/AoWRem0)




Deprescribing is the process of systematically identifying and discontinuing inappropriate medications (e.g., those no longer needed or with unfavorable risk-benefit profiles).




#### Identification and mitigation of barriers to <u>deprescribing</u> [[66]](/library/AoWRem0)[[67]](/library/jKW_Tm0)




* Ask specialists and colleagues why medications were started and whether they can be safely stopped.

* Set aside adequate time, e.g., a separate appointment, for <u>deprescribing</u>.

* Use <u>shared decision-making</u> to determine a patient's goals for continuing medications, e.g.: [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* <u>Primary prevention</u> or <u>secondary prevention</u>

* Slowing disease progression

* Preventing rapid decline

* Symptom management

* Ensure patients understand the benefits of <u>deprescribing</u> and address concerns, e.g.:

* Belief that a particular medication is necessary

* Concern that stopping a medication could precipitate withdrawal or worsen symptoms

* Worry that changes to their medication regimen may be difficult to understand or remember





> [!TIP]
> Multiple systemic factors also affect <u>deprescribing</u>, such as the absence of alternative medications in formularies, lack of financial incentives and resources, and limited clinician knowledge about the process and benefits of <u>deprescribing</u>. [[66]](/library/AoWRem0)[[67]](/library/jKW_Tm0)




#### Implementing a <u>deprescription</u> plan [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)[[66]](/library/AoWRem0)




* There is currently no standardized evidence-based approach to <u>deprescribing</u>; consider the following: [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)[[66]](/library/AoWRem0)

* If feasible, discontinue medications (one at a time) that have an unfavorable risk-benefit <u>ratio</u>.

* Discontinue medications that are least likely to have withdrawal reactions or rebound effects.

* Slowly taper any medications that can cause disease rebound or withdrawal. [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* Monitor patients closely (in person or remotely). [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)

* If medications cannot be discontinued, consider:

* Tapering to the lowest effective dose

* Switching to a safer alternative medication  [[68]](/library/pHWLr50)





> [!TIP]
> Stop one medication at a time to evaluate and document any unforeseen and/or negative consequences. [[57]](/library/l7cvNd0)
